prohibited_recommendations: Do not administer corticosteroids as monotherapy — they are ineffective in GBS.
Do not start IVIG without IgA-deficiency screening and renal function review.
Do not use neuromuscular-junction-blocking sedatives without securing the airway first.
required_recommendations: Admit for monitored bedrest with serial respiratory and autonomic checks every 4–6 hours.
Initiate IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (or plasma exchange) within 2 weeks of symptom onset.
Continuous cardiac telemetry for autonomic arrhythmias.
Repeat EMG/NCS in 1–2 weeks to delineate AIDP vs AMSAN given anti-GM1 / GD1a positivity.
DVT prophylaxis appropriate for immobilised inpatient.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Functional / metabolic brain imaging adds no value in a peripheral demyelinating syndrome.
Cerebrovascular imaging is not indicated in a peripheral neuropathy without focal cerebral signs.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP with secondary axonal injury (post-Campylobacter)

differential.key_features: Anti-GM1/GD1a IgG positivity and reduced CMAP amplitudes raise the possibility — partially explained as secondary axonal injury complicating AIDP rather than primary axonal disease.
Current short course cannot distinguish — re-evaluate at 4–8 weeks; persistent progression beyond 8 weeks would reclassify.
Patient is community-onset, not ICU-acquired; sensory involvement and antecedent infection point away from CIP.
Possible mimic if endemic exposure; Lyme serology testing covers; current serology supports Campylobacter.
Pattern is symmetric, not asymmetric/multifocal; no systemic vasculitis features.

key_clinical_evidence: Brighton level 1: progressive bilateral weakness + areflexia + EMG demyelinating + CSF albuminocytologic dissociation.
Antecedent Campylobacter and anti-GM1 / GD1a positivity flag a higher risk of axonal damage and a longer recovery.
Respiratory and autonomic monitoring drive disposition decisions even when bedside FVC is initially reassuring.
Acute-onset CIDP can mimic GBS; the divergence appears beyond 8 weeks — plan reassessment.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Residual inflammation from the antecedent Campylobacter infection — does not change the post-infectious autoimmune diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor the clinician on an ongoing infectious process.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

patient.chief_complaint: Eight-day progressive ascending weakness and sensory loss with bilateral facial weakness and areflexia, preceded by gastroenteritis.

social_history.living_situation: Single, lives alone; sister staying with her now

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. J. is a 42-year-old nurse presenting with an 8-day history of progressive ascending neurological symptoms. Three weeks ago she had a gastrointestinal illness with diarrhea lasting 4 days, which resolved. One week later, she noticed bilateral foot tingling. As a nurse, she was appropriately alarmed and came to the ED when she noticed difficulty rising from the toilet two days ago. Over the past 8 days, weakness has ascended from her feet to her thighs. She noted bilateral facial weakness when brushing her teeth this morning — both sides of her face are affected. She has difficulty swallowing thin liquids and has been coughing with water. She denies shortness of breath at rest but feels slightly breathless with exertion. She has no sphincter symptoms. She denies any tick exposure. Her prior flu vaccination was 3 months ago. Symptoms have been relentlessly progressive.
